profiles.title: Blanco tequila, Tequila Valley style
profiles.context: Unaged tequila from 100% blue agave, born in the town of Tequila and the valley that carries its name. Ask anyone from the valley: their agave grows smaller and more herbaceous than highland agave, and their blancos read savory and vegetal rather than sweet — the taste of this ground, and valley folk will tell you so with pride.
profiles.description: A blanco (also called silver or plata) is tequila that is bottled without oak aging, so what you taste is the distilled character of the cooked agave itself: roasted piña, citrus, pepper and fresh vegetal notes. Traditional valley producers often crush the cooked agave with a tahona stone wheel and ferment in open tanks, which adds texture and a savory, earthy edge that is typical of the region. This is editorial style guidance, not a rating of any specific bottle.
profiles.finish: Clean and peppery, with citrus and a gentle vegetal warmth that fades steadily.
profiles.plant: Agave tequilana Weber azul (blue weber agave, cultivated)
profiles.process: Steam-cooked (oven/autoclave), tahona or roller-mill extraction, fermented in open tanks, double distilled, unaged (blanco)
profiles.category: Tequila — spirit with its own Denomination of Origin; blanco is an unaged legal class
profiles.beginnerNote: New to tequila? A blanco is the unaged version — the purest read on cooked agave, before any oak influence. This is where every tequilero wants their land to speak first.

pairing.serving: Neat in a small glass or with a lime wheel; also the classic Margarita and Paloma base. Editorial suggestion, not a rule.

profiles.title: Espadín mezcal, Valles Centrales style
profiles.context: Artisanal joven mezcal made from espadín agave (Agave angustifolia) in the Valles Centrales around Oaxaca. Here mezcal is family work: agave hearts roasted in earthen pit ovens, small batches, generations of the same hands. The pit roast gives the spirit its signature smoke — in the Valles Centrales nobody calls that a flaw; they call it home. Espadín is the most widely planted mezcal agave and is often described as the most approachable of the common varieties.
profiles.description: Mezcal is a distilled spirit made from the roasted hearts of many agave species, not just blue agave. Roasting the piñas underground gives mezcal its characteristic smoke, layered over fruit, herb and mineral notes that vary with the agave variety, the village and the maestro mezcalero. This profile describes the style of a typical Valles Centrales espadín joven; individual bottles vary widely. This is editorial style guidance, not a rating of any specific bottle.
profiles.smoke: Gentle to moderate smoke from the pit-roast, woven through the fruit and herb notes rather than dominating them.
profiles.finish: Long and dry, with smoke that lingers softly and fades into earthy herbs.
profiles.process: Earthen-pit roast, tahona or horse-drawn mill, wild-yeast fermentation, double distilled, joven (unaged)
profiles.category: Mezcal — spirit with its own Denomination of Origin; joven/abocado is an unaged legal class
profiles.beginnerNote: New to mezcal? The smoke comes from roasting the agave underground — it is a character of the process, not an added flavor. Oaxacans will happily tell you it is the taste of their earth.

pairing.serving: Sipped neat at room temperature; smoke opens up in a wide glass. Editor's suggestion only.

profiles.title: Bacanora, Agave Pacifica style (Sierra de Sonora)
profiles.context: Ask a Sonoran about bacanora and watch their chest. This is our spirit, they will say — a wild agave spirit of the Sierra Madre de Sonora, distilled from Agave angustifolia pacifica (we just call it Pacifica, or Yaquiana) under a denomination of origin that covers 35 Sonoran municipalities. For most of the 20th century (1915–1992) making it was a crime, and Sonorans kept distilling anyway, hidden in the Sierra; the DO arrived in 2000. That stubbornness is the pride: bacanora survived because families refused to let it die.
profiles.description: Traditional bacanora roasts the agave hearts in earthen pit ovens, often with mesquite wood, ferments with wild yeasts and distills twice, giving a spirit that sits stylistically between tequila and Oaxacan mezcal: roasted agave at the center with smoke that is usually gentler than mezcal's, plus desert herbs and a mineral edge from the Sierra. This is editorial style guidance, not a rating of any specific bottle.
profiles.plant: Agave angustifolia pacifica (wild-harvested; locally Pacifica or Yaquiana)
profiles.process: Pit-roasted (often mesquite-fueled), wild-yeast fermentation, double distillation
profiles.category: Bacanora — spirit with its own Denomination of Origin (Sonora, since 2000)
profiles.beginnerNote: New to bacanora? Think of it as mezcal's Sonoran cousin — same roasted-agave heart, usually a touch less smoky, often leaner and more herbal. Sonorans will tell you it needs no introduction; they are right, but this helps.
profiles.smoke: Present but usually gentler than Oaxacan mezcal: the pit roast gives a lean, savory smoke rather than a dominant one.
profiles.finish: Dry and herbal, with a soft smoky thread and a mineral, peppery fade.

pairing.serving: Sipped neat, Sonoran-style with lime and a pinch of sal de chapulín; editorial suggestion.

profiles.title: Sierra raicilla, Maximiliana style (Jalisco)
profiles.context: Raicilla is the mountain spirit of Jalisco (the DO also reaches one Nayarit municipality, awarded in 2019), and jaliscienses wear it as proof their state makes more than tequila. It splits into two editorial traditions: Sierra (mountain) raicilla, made mainly from Agave maximiliana and inaequidens cooked in above-ground ovens, and Costa (coastal) raicilla from angustifolia and rhodacantha cooked in underground pits. For decades raicilla was distilled informally, in the shadow of its famous neighbor — locals kept it alive until the law caught up. This profile covers the Sierra style around the Sierra Occidental.
profiles.description: Sierra raicilla is typically cooked in above-ground adobe ovens rather than pits, so it tends to be less smoky than pit-roasted agave spirits, with a distinctive fermented, gently funky character: orchard fruit, herbs and a soft lactic roundness from wild-yeast fermentation in wooden vats. Distillation is often in small rustic stills (tabernas), and each maestro's batches vary widely. This is editorial style guidance, not a rating of any specific bottle.
profiles.plant: Agave maximiliana (wild-harvested; Sierra raicilla's signature agave)
profiles.process: Above-ground adobe-oven roast, open wild-yeast fermentation in wooden vats, small-batch distillation
profiles.category: Raicilla — spirit with its own Denomination of Origin (Jalisco and Bahía de Banderas, Nayarit, since 2019)
profiles.beginnerNote: New to raicilla? Expect an agave spirit that is often funkier and fruitier than tequila, and usually lighter on smoke than mezcal — Sierra versions especially. Jalisco's other pride, in a glass.
profiles.smoke: Usually light in the Sierra style: above-ground ovens give a faint roast note rather than pit smoke.
profiles.finish: Medium-long, gently funky, with orchard fruit and a soft sweet-agave fade.

pairing.serving: Sipped neat; its gentle funk also works in a Negroni-style serve (editorial suggestion).

profiles.title: Tuxca, Liñeno/Cimarrón style (Jalisco–Colima borderlands)
profiles.context: Tuxca is a borderlands spirit: a traditional agave distillate of the southern-Jalisco/northern-Colima frontier, named for the municipality of Tuxcacuesco below the Volcán de Colima. It has no denomination of origin, and the people who make it will tell you that is the point — the name is a regional tradition, not a legal category like tequila or mezcal, and definitions are loose. A working description centers production on the Río Almería valley near Tuxcacuesco, with Zapotitlán de Vadillo and Tolimán forming the historical heartland. In these villages the tradition is kept the old way, and quietly.
profiles.description: Tuxca is defined less by a legal category than by its method: wild agaves (often Liñeno/Cimarrón, i.e. Agave angustifolia and relatives) roasted in cylindrical pits, hand-mashed, fermented in volcanic stone craters, and distilled in wooden Filipino stills. The result is lean, spicy and mineral rather than smoky-sweet. This is editorial style guidance, not a rating of any specific bottle.
profiles.plant: Wild agaves, often Liñeno/Cimarrón (Agave angustifolia and local relatives); ensambles vary by vinatero
profiles.process: Cylindrical pit roast, hand-mash, volcanic crater fermentation, wooden Filipino still distillation
profiles.category: Tuxca — a regional tradition with no denomination of origin; legal status is not equivalent to tequila or mezcal
profiles.beginnerNote: New to tuxca? Expect an uncertified, deeply traditional borderlands spirit — leaner and more mineral than most mezcal, with spice instead of smoke. No seal on the bottle; pride is the certificate.
profiles.smoke: Usually light: the pit roast is shorter and the wooden stills read herbal-spicy rather than smoky.
profiles.finish: Dry and spicy, with lime and pepper fading to volcanic mineral.

pairing.serving: Sipped neat alongside water; lean and mineral, it suits slow sipping (editorial suggestion).

profiles.title: Comiteco, aguamiel style (Comitán, Chiapas)
profiles.context: Comiteco belongs to Comitán de Dománguez, Chiapas, and chiapanecos speak of it as theirs alone: a sap-derived agave spirit where, instead of cooking harvested agave hearts, producers collect the fresh sap (aguamiel) of the living maguey Comiteco (Agave atrovirens), ferment it, and distill it. Some comiteco includes an additional cane-based sugar source; a proposal to define the category sets a minimum of agave content rather than requiring 100% agave. Whether a specific bottle is 100% agave is a separate fact from its eligibility for this app — agave-based traditions with verified, clearly disclosed non-agave ingredients are included honestly.
profiles.description: Because the agave is never cooked, comiteco lacks the roast and smoke of pit-roasted spirits and instead shows a green, lactic, gently herbal character carried over from the fermented sap — closer in character to a distilled pulque than to mezcal, though it is its own tradition. This profile describes the style generally; compositions vary between producers and are disclosed per bottle. This is editorial style guidance, not a rating of any specific bottle.
profiles.plant: Maguey Comiteco (Agave atrovirens), cultivated; sap collected from the living plant
profiles.process: Sap-derived: aguamiel collected from the living plant, fermented, distilled — no cooking of the piña
profiles.category: Comiteco — a regional tradition from Comitán, Chiapas; not a spirit with a denomination of origin, and not legally equivalent to tequila or mezcal
profiles.beginnerNote: New to comiteco? Forget smoke: this is a sap spirit — think green, lactic and herbal, from uncooked agave. Comitán's own tradition, unlike anything to the north.
profiles.finish: Smooth and herbal, with a light earthy fade and no roast character.

pairing.serving: Sipped neat; traditionally a small-occasion spirit — editorial suggestion only.

profiles.title: Destilado de pulque, Salmiana style (Tlaxcala)
profiles.context: Tlaxcala holds pulque close: it is the heartland of the maguey pulquero. Destilado de pulque is the region's distilled agave-sap spirit — producers of the pulque tradition ferment the aguamiel of the maguey pulquero (Agave salmiana) into pulque, then distill it — the agave is never cooked. Tlaxcala is not part of the mezcal denomination, and destilado de pulque is not a certified category; it is a regional tradition, sold under destilado labels, kept by families who consider distilling pulque a birthright of their hills. Fermented pulque itself (undistilled) is not part of this spirit catalogue.
profiles.description: Distilling a fermented sap rather than a cooked agave mash gives destilado de pulque its signature: fresh, green, lactic and faintly wild, with the vegetal, slightly tangy character of pulque carried into the glass rather than roast or smoke. Reviews note everything from steamed grass and sour-candy acidity to creamed-corn sweetness — a broad, unusual range. This is editorial style guidance, not a rating of any specific bottle.
profiles.plant: Maguey pulquero (Agave salmiana); sap collected daily from the living plant
profiles.process: Sap-derived: aguamiel fermented into pulque (about 48 hours), then distilled; the piña is never cooked
profiles.category: Destilado de pulque — a regional tradition; no denomination of origin, and explicitly not mezcal (fermented pulque is not a spirit and is not catalogued here)
profiles.beginnerNote: New to destilado de pulque? It is distilled pulque — uncooked agave sap, so expect lactic, green, gently sour character unlike any cooked-agave spirit. A taste of Tlaxcala's oldest trade.
profiles.finish: Light and tangy, with lactic and green notes that fade quickly.

pairing.serving: Sipped neat, chilled slightly; its lactic tang suits an open mind (editorial suggestion).

profiles.title: Costa raicilla, coastal style (Jalisco)
profiles.context: Raicilla's denomination of origin (2019) spans 16 Jalisco municipalities and one in Nayarit, and editorially splits into two traditions: Sierra (mountain) and Costa (coastal). Coastal raicilla comes from the Cabo Corrientes and Tomatlán area, made mainly with Agave angustifolia (locally chico aguiar) and Agave rhodacantha. Fishermen and farmers on this coast cook their agave in underground pits, the old way — and they will tell you their raicilla has salt in its soul that the mountains cannot match.
profiles.description: Unlike the Sierra style's above-ground adobe ovens, coastal producers traditionally cook their agave in underground pits — so coastal raicilla leans smokier and more savory than its mountain sibling, with the pit roast alongside citrus and herbal notes. This profile describes the editorial style; individual bottles vary widely and tasting notes for the example bottle are not yet documented. This is editorial style guidance, not a rating of any specific bottle.
profiles.plant: Agave angustifolia (chico aguiar) and Agave rhodacantha (wild and cultivated)
profiles.process: Underground pit roast, wild-yeast fermentation, small-batch distillation
profiles.category: Raicilla — spirit with its own Denomination of Origin (Jalisco and Bahía de Banderas, Nayarit, since 2019); Costa is an editorial tradition split, not a legal class
profiles.beginnerNote: New to coastal raicilla? Think of it as the smokier seaside cousin of Sierra raicilla: same DO, different cook. The coast's own pride.
profiles.smoke: More present than in Sierra raicilla: the underground pit cook gives a savory smoke woven through citrus and herbs.
profiles.finish: Medium-long, smoky and savory with a citrus fade.

pairing.serving: Sipped neat; the smoke suits slow evening sipping (editorial suggestion).

profiles.title: Reposado tequila, Tequila Valley style
profiles.context: Reposado ('rested') is a legal tequila class: the spirit rests in oak for a minimum of two months, with no maximum. In practice most producers rest it two months to a year. This profile describes a traditionally made Tequila Valley reposado — the same style as this app's blanco profile, plus oak. Valley tradition holds that rest should season the agave, never bury it; that restraint is local pride.
profiles.description: Reposado is where tequila first meets wood: the vegetal, peppery blanco character takes on vanilla, caramel and baking-spice notes from the barrel while the cooked agave stays at the center. In traditionally made reposados the oak is a seasoning, not the dish — reviewers of the example bottle consistently note the agave remains forward. There is no universal age-to-flavor ladder: a 2-month reposado can read leaner than a blanco from another producer, and 'more oak' is not 'better'. This is editorial style guidance, not a rating of any specific bottle.
profiles.plant: Agave tequilana Weber azul (blue weber agave, cultivated)
profiles.process: Steam-cooked, fermented, double distilled, then rested in oak barrels (legal minimum 2 months; typically 2–12 months)
profiles.category: Tequila — spirit with its own Denomination of Origin; reposado is a legal class (oak-rested, 2-month minimum)
profiles.beginnerNote: New to reposado? Think of it as the same spirit as blanco, briefly rested in oak: the agave stays, vanilla and spice join.
profiles.finish: Medium, with gentle wood spice and a caramel-agave fade.

pairing.serving: Sipped neat; also the classic Margarita upgrade for those who want a rounder base (editorial suggestion).

profiles.title: Añejo tequila, Tequila Valley style
profiles.context: Añejo ('aged') is a legal tequila class: oak rest of at least one year, in barrels of no more than 600 liters. Extra añejo (at least three years) exists as a further class. This profile describes a traditionally made Valley añejo of roughly 18 months — the middle of the legal range. In the valley they will tell you the agave should still speak through a year of oak; the best producers make sure it does.
profiles.description: A year or more of oak turns tequila darker, rounder and sweeter-perceived: the barrel contributes vanilla, dried fruit and cocoa-adjacent notes while the fresh vegetal edge of the blanco recedes. A well-made añejo keeps cooked agave in the frame rather than disappearing into wood; the example bottle's reviewers describe exactly that balance. 'Older is better' is marketing, not a rule — wood influence depends on barrel type, size, age and climate, and many drinkers prefer blanco or reposado. This is editorial style guidance, not a rating of any specific bottle.
profiles.plant: Agave tequilana Weber azul (blue weber agave, cultivated)
profiles.process: Steam-cooked, fermented, double distilled, then aged in oak at least one year (typically ex-bourbon casks)
profiles.category: Tequila — spirit with its own Denomination of Origin; añejo is a legal class (oak-aged, 1-year minimum)
profiles.beginnerNote: New to añejo? Expect the roundest, darkest tequila expression: oak-driven vanilla and dried fruit around the agave — closest to whiskey in feel, still tequila at heart.
profiles.finish: Long and rounded, with oak spice, sweet agave and a gentle dry fade.

pairing.serving: Sipped neat, ideally in a small glass to concentrate the aroma (editorial suggestion).

profiles.title: Cristalino tequila style
profiles.context: Cristalino is not a legal class: it is an aged tequila (usually reposado or añejo) filtered — typically through wood charcoal — to remove the color the barrel gave it. Nearly every major brand now makes one. The category is commercially booming and critically debated: bartenders and writers are divided over whether it is innovation or a marketing-driven dilution of tradition — and that debate is itself part of how Mexico argues, with pride, about its spirits.
profiles.description: A cristalino looks like a blanco in the glass but carries softened barrel character: rounder, creamier and often sweeter-perceived than either a blanco or its unfiltered aged base, with gentler acidity and agave bite. Filtration removes color and, with it, some flavor — what remains is by design smooth and approachable. The category is prone to additive use to restore sweetness and body, which critics flag; the base spirit and the producer matter more than the style name. This is editorial style guidance, not a rating of any specific bottle.
profiles.plant: Agave tequilana Weber azul (blue weber agave, cultivated)
profiles.process: Made as oak-rested reposado or añejo, then charcoal-filtered clear; a finishing choice, not a legal class
profiles.category: Cristalino — a finishing/marketing style on top of a legal class, not a legal class itself; disclosure of the aged base varies by brand
profiles.beginnerNote: New to cristalino? It is an aged tequila with the color filtered out — clear like a blanco, rounder like an añejo, and the subject of honest debate.
profiles.finish: Smooth and short-to-medium; engineered for easy sipping.

placeCoords.precision: region (Jalisco, highlands/valley varies by producer); approximate

pairing.serving: Served neat or over ice; often positioned as an entry to aged tequila (editorial suggestion).

profiles.title: Comiteco añejo, glass-rested with oak branches (Comitán, Chiapas)
profiles.context: Comiteco is a sap-derived agave spirit from the municipality of Comitán de Domínguez, Chiapas, produced by fermenting and distilling the fresh sap (aguamiel) of the living maguey Comiteco (Agave atrovirens) without cooking the plant. This profile covers the aged expression of that tradition. Unlike tequila or mezcal añejo, comiteco añejo is not a legally defined class: the añejo of the example producer rests in glass with branches of white oak rather than in barrels, so its wood character comes from oak contact in glass, not barrel maturation. In Comitán that oak-branch rest is an art passed through generations — chiapaneco patience in a bottle. The broader category has no denomination of origin, though a state request for DO protection has been in process.
profiles.description: Glass resting on white-oak branches gives this style a soft wood influence without the vanilla-heavy roundness of barrel-aged spirits: the green, lactic, herbal sap character of comiteco stays in the frame while oak contributes gentle spice and a touch of color. Compared with the unaged comiteco profile, expect a slightly rounder, warmer version of the same tradition rather than a whiskey-adjacent profile. This is editorial style guidance, not a rating of any specific bottle.
profiles.plant: Maguey Comiteco (Agave atrovirens), cultivated; sap collected from the living plant
profiles.process: Sap-derived: aguamiel collected from the living plant, fermented, distilled in copper, then rested in glass with branches of white oak (no barrel maturation, no cooking of the piña)
profiles.category: Comiteco añejo — a regional tradition from Comitán, Chiapas; not a spirit with a denomination of origin, and añejo here is a producer expression, not a legal class as it is in tequila
profiles.beginnerNote: New to comiteco añejo? Do not expect tequila añejo: the wood comes from oak branches resting in glass, so it is gentler — think warm spice over the same green, lactic sap character.
profiles.finish: Medium-length and herbal, with a soft oak-spice fade and no roast character.

pairing.serving: Sipped neat to let the gentle oak spice carry the herbal sap character (editorial suggestion).

profiles.title: Raicilla reposado, barrel-rested style (Jalisco)
profiles.context: Raicilla is a denomination-of-origin agave spirit from Jalisco, and unlike comiteco or destilado de pulque it does carry legally defined aged classes: reposado means a rest in wood. This profile covers the young-rested end of that range — short rests of a few months that round the spirit without pushing the agave out of the frame. Jalisco's raicilleros are proud that their spirit earned legal recognition without giving up its rustic character; short rests are how they keep it that way.
profiles.description: A short barrel rest (the example bottle lists 3 months) takes the fruity, floral, delicately smoky raicilla character and adds a light wood halo: vanilla, caramel and soft fruit sweetness around — rather than instead of — the agave. Reviewers of the example bottle describe sherry-cask influence with plum, raisin and sweet tobacco, and note the agave can be overpowered by cask character; that risk of wood masking the spirit is part of this style's honest picture. This is editorial style guidance, not a rating of any specific bottle.
profiles.plant: Varies by bottling (the example bottle lists Angustifolia and Maximiliana); linked to the Maximiliana plant page as the Sierra tradition's signature agave — check the bottle, batches differ
profiles.process: Fermented and distilled (the example bottle lists steel), then rested in wooden barrels about 3 months
profiles.category: Raicilla reposado — a legally defined aged class under the raicilla denomination of origin (minimum 2 months in wood per the cited DO source)
profiles.beginnerNote: New to aged raicilla? Expect the fruit and florals of the joven with a light caramel-vanilla halo from a short rest — closer to its unaged self than to tequila reposado.
profiles.smoke: A delicate smokiness can persist from production; the example bottle's reviewer notes campfire smoke on the finish.
profiles.finish: Medium to long, with sweet fruit, cinnamon-adjacent spice and a soft smoke fade.

pairing.serving: Sipped neat; a short-rested raicilla also works where a fruity reposado is called for (editorial suggestion).

profiles.title: Extra añejo tequila, highland style (Jalisco)
profiles.context: Extra añejo ('extra aged') is the newest legal tequila class: a minimum of three years in oak barrels of no more than 600 liters, added to the NOM in 2006. It exists because producers wanted recognition for long-rested tequilas; El Tesoro's family released its Paradiso in 1994, before the class legally existed. This profile describes a highland extra añejo of four to five years — the longer side of the legal range. Highland pride runs deep here: highland agave grows bigger and sweeter, and alteños say it is the only agave that can carry that much oak and still taste of agave.
profiles.description: Three-plus years of oak pushes tequila toward brandy territory: deep oak, chocolate, coffee and dried fruit around a cooked-agave core. The honest tension of this class is that many producers consider more than about four years excessive — wood can overwhelm the delicate agave — so the best extra añejos are those that keep agave in the frame, as the example bottle's reviewers note. 'Older is better' remains marketing, not a rule. This is editorial style guidance, not a rating of any specific bottle.
profiles.plant: Agave tequilana Weber azul (blue weber agave, cultivated; highland mineral soils)
profiles.process: Steam-cooked (or stone-roasted by some traditionalists), fermented, double distilled, then aged at least three years in oak (typically American ex-bourbon barrels)
profiles.category: Tequila — spirit with its own Denomination of Origin; extra añejo is a legal class (oak-aged, 3-year minimum, barrels up to 600 liters)
profiles.beginnerNote: New to extra añejo? This is tequila at its most whiskey-adjacent: expect oak, chocolate and coffee — the good ones still taste of agave underneath.
profiles.finish: Long and oaky, with chocolate, gentle spice and a slow agave fade.

pairing.serving: Sipped neat after dinner, in a snifter-style glass (editorial suggestion).

profiles.title: Mezcal reposado, briefly barrel-rested espadín style (Valles Centrales, Oaxaca)
profiles.context: Reposado is a legal mezcal class (the NOM recognizes joven, reposado and añejo): a rest of two months to a year in oak. Most mezcal sold worldwide is joven (unaged), and many Oaxacan traditionalists argue wood obscures what makes mezcal distinct — that argument is part of the pride: they defend their pit roast because it is their land in the glass. Aged mezcal is nonetheless a growing, legal part of the category. This profile covers the short-rested end: a few months in wood, typically starting from pit-roasted espadín.
profiles.description: A short barrel rest softens the pit-roast smoke of espadín mezcal and layers light vanilla and caramel over it, without erasing the spirit's vegetal, roasted character. Reviews of the example bottle describe exactly that balance — smoke carried from nose to finish, ending in a smoky butterscotch — while others caution the wood can dominate. Expect mezcal first, wood second; if the wood leads, it is closer to tequila reposado territory. This is editorial style guidance, not a rating of any specific bottle.
profiles.plant: Agave angustifolia (espadín, cultivated); some producers blend wild agaves
profiles.process: Pit-roasted, stone-milled, wild-fermented, distilled, then rested in oak 2-12 months (the example bottle lists 4-6 months in American oak)
profiles.category: Mezcal — spirit with its own denomination of origin; reposado is a legal class (oak-rested, 2 months to 1 year)
profiles.beginnerNote: New to mezcal reposado? Expect the smoke of a joven softened with vanilla and caramel — a gentler entry into smoked agave spirits.
profiles.smoke: The pit-roast smoke of espadín mezcal persists through the rest; reviewers describe it from nose to finish.
profiles.finish: Medium, smoky-sweet, with a butterscotch-adjacent fade.

placeCoords.precision: region (Tlacolula valley, Valles Centrales, Oaxaca); approximate

pairing.serving: Sipped neat; also works in margaritas where a smoky reposado is welcome (editorial suggestion).

profiles.title: Tobalá mezcal, wild Agave potatorum style (Sierra, Oaxaca)
profiles.context: Tobalá (Agave potatorum) is a small, high-altitude, mostly wild agave often called the 'king of agaves' in México; its tiny size and 12-15 year maturity give very low yields, which has pushed prices up and wild populations down. The mezcal DO permits any agave species, so tobalá is mezcal; some tobalá is now cultivated, which changes both the sustainability story and, reviewers note, sometimes the flavor. This is a plant-driven style, not a place-driven one: tobalá grows across Oaxaca's Sierra Norte and beyond. In the Sierra Norte, finding a tobalá ready to harvest is a source of personal pride — a mezcalero will walk you to the plant, not to a map.
profiles.description: Tobalá mezcal is typically lighter and more floral than espadín, with sweet citrus, tropical fruit and a silky texture over a gentler roast. Batch variation is genuinely large — a cited blind tasting of eight tobalás found no single common thread — so treat this as a family of expressions, not one flavor. The example bottle, from 100% cultivated tobalá, shows lemon, pear and green pepper aromas with basil and roasted fig on the palate. This is editorial style guidance, not a rating of any specific bottle.
profiles.plant: Agave potatorum (tobalá; mostly wild-harvested, some cultivated — check the bottle)
profiles.process: Pit-roasted, stone-milled, wild-fermented, distilled (clay pot stills in ancestral productions, copper in artisanal ones)
profiles.category: Mezcal — tobalá is within the mezcal denomination of origin; it is a wild agave category under sustainability pressure, not a legal class of its own
profiles.beginnerNote: New to tobalá? Expect mezcal's gentler, more floral cousin: sweet citrus and tropical fruit over a soft roast — pricier because the agave is small, slow and scarce.
profiles.smoke: A gentle roast character rather than heavy smoke; ancestral clay-pot batches can show more.
profiles.finish: Medium and silky, with fruit sweetness and a soft mineral fade.

placeCoords.precision: region (Sierra Norte / Santiago Matatlán area, Oaxaca); approximate

pairing.serving: Sipped neat in a small copita; tobalá's florals fade in cocktails (editorial suggestion).

profiles.title: Sotol, Chihuahua desert style
profiles.context: Ask a sotolero what sotol is and you will hear it plainly: not agave, and proud of it. Sotol is distilled from plants of the Dasylirion genus (desert spoon), native to the Chihuahuan desert — relatives of agave in the Asparagaceae family that share the roasted-piña logic. Sotol has had a Denominación de Origen since 2002, covering only Chihuahua, Coahuila and Durango; it was illegal in Mexico before 1994, and clandestine vinatas kept the tradition alive, just as Sonoran families kept bacanora. This guide includes it as an agave-adjacent tradition, honestly labeled: sotol is not an agave spirit, and saying so is part of its story. This profile describes the Chihuahua desert style.
profiles.description: Sotol's signature is a bright, grassy, herbal, sometimes menthol- or eucalyptus-adjacent freshness — more vegetal than most agave spirits, with a smoky, earthy base from pit roasting. Terroir is unusually audible: the cited DO sources describe forested-region sotols tasting of menthol, mushrooms and pine, while arid-desert ones lean to leather, cacao and pepper. A single plant yields roughly one bottle after 8-12 years, so batches are small and vary genuinely. This is editorial style guidance, not a rating of any specific bottle.
profiles.plant: Dasylirion (desert spoon; commonly wheeleri, cedrosanum or leiophyllum), wild-harvested; not an agave, though a close relative
profiles.process: Piña pit-roasted in conical ovens (or steam-cooked by larger producers), wild-fermented, distilled in copper or clay; harvest can leave roots intact so the plant regrows
profiles.category: Sotol — spirit with its own Denomination of Origin (Chihuahua, Coahuila, Durango, since 2002); explicitly not an agave spirit, included here as an agave-adjacent northern tradition
profiles.beginnerNote: New to sotol? Expect bright wet-grass and herbal freshness over gentle smoke — closer to a green, wild cousin of mezcal than to tequila.
profiles.smoke: A gentle, usually lighter smoke than mezcal from the pit roast; batch and producer dependent.
profiles.finish: Medium, herbal and slightly tingly, with a mineral fade.

pairing.serving: Sipped neat in a small glass; also good with mineral sparkling water (editorial suggestion).
